item.text:
**Overview**

Nigeria had no nuclear weapons and no open nuclear-arsenal program in 2023. Under Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the relevant question is whether the government preserved or improved the country’s nonproliferation, nuclear-safety, biosecurity, cyber, and counterterrorism posture. The evidence points to a mostly inherited and continuity-based posture, with some rhetorical emphasis on security and later 2024 operational coordination, but no sign in 2023 of a major new catastrophic-risk doctrine or treaty shift.

Tinubu’s own inaugural speech made security a top priority, promised reform of doctrine and architecture, and explicitly linked foreign policy to peace and stability in West Africa and Africa. It also endorsed fuel-subsidy removal and a unified exchange rate, showing that his early agenda was concentrated on economic stabilization rather than any nuclear posture change. The strongest nuclear-related material in the record is therefore institutional and baseline: Nigeria’s long-standing NPT and IAEA safeguards commitments, plus later 2023 and 2024 government activity on biosecurity, cyber, counterterrorism, and regional security. ([statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/first-inaugural-address-by-president-bola-ahmed-tinubu-delivered-on-may-29-2023-at-the-eagle-square-abuja/), [ola.iaea.org](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG))

**Evidence Index**

1. **Inherited nonproliferation baseline**
- **Claim:** Nigeria was already a non-nuclear-weapon state with long-standing treaty and safeguards commitments before Tinubu took office, including NPT ratification and IAEA safeguards agreements. This matters because it defines the starting point for 2023: Tinubu inherited a nonproliferation framework rather than building one from scratch.
- **Best source:** UN Treaty Collection and IAEA Office of Legal Affairs country profile.  
  - UNTC NPT action record: [treaties.un.org](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/showActionDetails.aspx?clang=_en&objid=0800000280120b6a)  
  - IAEA Nigeria profile: [ola.iaea.org](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG)
- **Locator:** UNTC shows Nigeria’s ratification of the NPT; IAEA lists Nigeria’s safeguards agreement with the IAEA in connection with the NPT and the Additional Protocol, plus CPPNM/CPPNM-A and nuclear-safety conventions. ([treaties.un.org](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/showActionDetails.aspx?clang=_en&objid=0800000280120b6a), [ola.iaea.org](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG))
- **Period fit:** Inherited baseline.
- **Ruler attribution:** Weak direct attribution. This is pre-Tinubu legal posture, but it frames his inherited responsibility.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** None suggesting Nigeria possessed or sought nuclear weapons in 2023.
- **Caution:** Treaty participation does not by itself prove implementation quality.
- **Independent support:** IAEA country profile; UN treaty status pages.  

2. **No evidence of nuclear-weapon brinkmanship; rhetoric emphasized restraint and regional peace**
- **Claim:** In his May 29, 2023 inaugural address, Tinubu did not threaten nuclear force or normalize catastrophic escalation; instead he said security would be top priority, promised to reform security doctrine and architecture, and said foreign policy would prioritize peace and stability in West Africa and Africa. This matters because the ruler’s rhetoric is one of the few direct indicators available for catastrophic-risk posture in a non-nuclear state.
- **Best source:** State House, “First Inaugural Address by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu Delivered on May 29, 2023 at the Eagle Square, Abuja.”  
  Direct link: [statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/first-inaugural-address-by-president-bola-ahmed-tinubu-delivered-on-may-29-2023-at-the-eagle-square-abuja/)
- **Locator:** Lines 84-100 and 142-145. He states that security is the top priority, says the administration will reform the “security DOCTRINE and its ARCHITECTURE,” and says foreign policy’s primary objective must be peace and stability in the West African subregion and African continent. ([statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/first-inaugural-address-by-president-bola-ahmed-tinubu-delivered-on-may-29-2023-at-the-eagle-square-abuja/))
- **Period fit:** Target-period contemporaneous.
- **Ruler attribution:** Direct.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** Later 2024 security statements were much more hard-edged, including “treat kidnappers as terrorists,” but still conventional, not nuclear, escalation rhetoric. ([statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-we-must-treat-kidnappers-as-terrorist/))
- **Caution:** This is self-presentation in an inaugural speech, not evidence of implementation.
- **Independent support:** The same speech also commits to work with ECOWAS and the AU on conflicts, consistent with a de-escalatory regional posture.  

3. **Nigeria’s nuclear-regulatory and safeguards infrastructure remained in place**
- **Claim:** As of 2023, Nigeria remained inside the IAEA safeguards and nuclear-safety architecture, including the NPT safeguards agreement, Additional Protocol, Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material, Convention on Nuclear Safety, and accident-notification/assistance conventions. This matters because safe handling of any future nuclear program depends on this legal and institutional base.
- **Best source:** IAEA Office of Legal Affairs country profile for Nigeria.  
  Direct link: [ola.iaea.org](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG)
- **Locator:** Lines 18-25 list the safeguards and safety instruments. Lines 2-4 show IAEA membership since 1968; lines 21-26 list CPPNM, CPPNM/A, early-notification, assistance, and nuclear-safety commitments. ([ola.iaea.org](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG))
- **Period fit:** Inherited baseline, relevant throughout 2023.
- **Ruler attribution:** Weak direct attribution; the commitments predate Tinubu, but his government inherited them.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** IAEA legal status does not show implementation quality or enforcement effectiveness in 2023.
- **Caution:** This is a formal-commitments record, not an operational-performance record.
- **Independent support:** UNTC NPT ratification record.  

4. **Biosecurity policy was already approved, and Tinubu inherited a formal counter-biothreat framework**
- **Claim:** Nigeria entered Tinubu’s presidency with an approved National Biosecurity Policy and Action Plan for 2022-2026, designed for prevention, early detection, rapid response, and recovery from biosecurity incidents through a One Health approach. This matters because biosecurity is one of the main catastrophic dual-use risk areas relevant to Nigeria.
- **Best source:** National Biosafety Management Agency announcement of federal approval.  
  Direct link: [nbma.gov.ng](https://nbma.gov.ng/fg-approves-a-national-biosecurity-policy-for-nigeria/)
- **Locator:** Lines 20-35. The Federal Executive Council approved the policy; it aims at protection from harmful biological agents, a One Health approach, and prevention/rapid response to biothreats. ([nbma.gov.ng](https://nbma.gov.ng/fg-approves-a-national-biosecurity-policy-for-nigeria/))
- **Period fit:** Inherited baseline, still operative in 2023.
- **Ruler attribution:** Moderate as inherited responsibility, not a Tinubu-created policy.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** Approval is not the same as sustained budgeted implementation.
- **Caution:** NBMA text is official self-reporting and promotional in tone.
- **Independent support:** NBMA’s related unveiling page and WHO remarks on the same policy. ([nbma.gov.ng](https://nbma.gov.ng/minister-of-environment-calls-for-concerted-effort-in-the-bid-to-protect-nigerians-from-harmful-biological-agents-unveils-approved-biosecurity-policy-document/))

5. **Nigeria had formal 1540 nonproliferation obligations and an implementation framework, but the public record did not show a Tinubu-era leap in 2023**
- **Claim:** UN Security Council resolution 1540 requires states to stop non-state actors from developing or acquiring nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons, and the UN 1540 system tracks national implementation plans and matrices. Nigeria was already part of this architecture before Tinubu, but the public sources inspected here did not show a clearly new 2023 Tinubu-specific action plan or major legal upgrade. This matters because 1540 is the main UN framework for non-state proliferator control.
- **Best source:** UN 1540 Committee pages.  
  Direct links: [un.org national implementation plans](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/national-implementation-plans.shtml), [UN 1540 FAQ](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/faq.shtml), [UN 1540 matrices](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/1540-matrices.shtml), [national reports](https://static.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/national-reports.shtml)
- **Locator:** The FAQ states states must adopt and enforce laws preventing non-state actors from acquiring or using nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons. The matrices page explains that approved matrices summarize implementation measures, and the national-reports page lists Nigeria’s 2004 submission history. ([un.org](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/faq.shtml), [un.org](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/1540-matrices.shtml), [static.un.org](https://static.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/national-reports.shtml))
- **Period fit:** Inherited baseline; no decisive 2023 change detected in the inspected sources.
- **Ruler attribution:** Weak direct attribution.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** Later UN documents show Nigeria continued engagement with 1540-related capacity-building, but that evidence is outside 2023 and does not by itself prove Tinubu-era improvement.
- **Caution:** The inspected UN pages are framework and registry pages, not a Nigeria-specific 2023 implementation audit.
- **Independent support:** UNODA 1540 resources and the national-report registry.

6. **Government attention to cyber and terrorism risk was real, but mostly as broad security administration rather than existential-risk governance**
- **Claim:** The National Counter Terrorism Centre’s materials show Nigeria had a national cyber-security policy and a national security strategy on the books, and Tinubu publicly prioritized security cooperation and counterterrorism. This matters because cyber and terrorism are the only catastrophic-risk-adjacent areas where the 2023 record shows active executive attention.
- **Best sources:** NCTC books index and State House statements.  
  Direct links: [NCTC books](https://nctc.gov.ng/books/), [NCTC National Cyber Security Policy](https://nctc.gov.ng/books/national-cyber-security-policy/), [NCTC NSS 2019](https://nctc.gov.ng/books/national-security-strategy-nss-2019/), [Tinubu/FBI statement](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-meets-fbi-director-calls-for-stronger-collaboration-to-fight-cybercrime-and-terrorism/)
- **Locator:** NCTC’s books page lists “NATIONAL CYBER SECURITY POLICY,” “National Security Strategy (NSS 2019),” and terrorism-prevention materials. The FBI statement says Tinubu called for stronger collaboration to fight cybercrime, terrorism, and related crimes. ([nctc.gov.ng](https://nctc.gov.ng/books/), [statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-meets-fbi-director-calls-for-stronger-collaboration-to-fight-cybercrime-and-terrorism/))
- **Period fit:** Mostly target-period and immediate follow-on.
- **Ruler attribution:** Moderate for the cooperation agenda; weaker for the underlying policy documents, which predate him.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** The public evidence opened here does not show that 2023 cyber or terrorism policy materially reduced catastrophic risk; it shows administrative continuity and cross-border cooperation.
- **Caution:** The NCTC books page is an index, not a policy implementation audit.
- **Independent support:** State House 2024 security briefing and New Year address, which both frame security as central and ongoing. ([statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/text-of-president-bola-ahmed-tinubus-new-year-address-to-the-nation/), [statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-to-security-chiefs-you-are-making-good-progress-but-there-must-be-conclusive-victory/))

7. **Tinubu’s 2024 rhetoric confirms security centrality but not a nuclear posture shift**
- **Claim:** In January 2024 Tinubu said the government was working to free captives, that it had not solved all security problems, and that it was pursuing peace and stability. In March 2024 he said kidnappers should be treated as terrorists. This matters because it shows continuity in security rhetoric, but nothing specifically about nuclear or other existential-risk doctrine.
- **Best sources:** State House New Year address and later security statements.  
  Direct links: [New Year address](https://statehouse.gov.ng/text-of-president-bola-ahmed-tinubus-new-year-address-to-the-nation/), [kidnappers as terrorists](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-we-must-treat-kidnappers-as-terrorist/), [security chiefs briefing](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-to-security-chiefs-you-are-making-good-progress-but-there-must-be-conclusive-victory/)
- **Locator:** The New Year address says the government removed fuel subsidy and foreign exchange distortions, is working to free captives, and is seeking peace and stability. The March 2024 statement says kidnappers should be treated as terrorists. ([statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/text-of-president-bola-ahmed-tinubus-new-year-address-to-the-nation/), [statehouse.gov.ng](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-we-must-treat-kidnappers-as-terrorist/))
- **Period fit:** Slightly later retrospective, but still close to the period under review.
- **Ruler attribution:** Direct.
- **Contrary/complicating evidence:** This rhetoric is coercive and domestic-focused; it does not evidence careful existential-risk governance.
- **Caution:** These are speeches, not implementation records.

**Disposition by Lens**

- **1B.1 Reducing existential risk:** Partial evidence only. Tinubu’s rhetoric favored stability and regional peace, but there is no 2023 evidence of a distinct existential-risk-reduction program.
- **1B.10 Lasting risk posture:** Unclear. The inherited nonproliferation and biosecurity framework remained in place; no strong 2023 evidence shows durable improvement.
- **1B.2 Responsible nuclear rhetoric:** Satisfied at a baseline level. No reckless nuclear rhetoric found; his public statements were conventional security language.
- **1B.3 Safe nuclear control:** Mostly inherited baseline. Nigeria had safeguards and safety commitments, but no Tinubu-era nuclear-custody record.
- **1B.4 Arms control and inspections:** Baseline commitments present; no 2023 upgrade or degradation identified.
- **1B.5 Nuclear cover for aggression:** No evidence found that Tinubu used any nuclear capability for coercion or repression. Nigeria has no nuclear arsenal.
- **1B.6 Preventing proliferation:** Baseline legal controls exist through 1540 and treaty commitments; no 2023 enforcement record found.
- **1B.7 Independent risk expertise:** Limited evidence. The public record here shows reliance on established agencies, not a major expert-appointment story.
- **1B.8 Crisis de-escalation:** Some evidence of de-escalatory regional language and conventional security management, but no existential-crisis case.
- **1B.9 Other catastrophic risks:** Most relevant area in this chapter. Nigeria had biosecurity, cyber, and counterterrorism frameworks, but the 2023 evidence shows continuity rather than a clearly new or measured Tinubu reform.

**Information Environment**

- Information quality was much better for formal treaties, agency structure, and presidential rhetoric than for actual implementation.
- The weakest area is operational verification: whether biosecurity, cyber, and counterterrorism controls were funded, staffed, and enforced effectively in 2023.
- Official pages are useful for formal posture but tend to overstate progress.
- The UN 1540 pages are strong for legal framework and registry status but weak for country-level performance.
- This chapter is not about nuclear weapons in the narrow sense; it is mainly about whether Tinubu’s government strengthened or weakened dual-use and catastrophic-risk governance. On that question, the evidence supports continuity with modest security emphasis, not a transformative shift.

**Research Gaps**

- Whether Tinubu made any 2023 appointment that materially changed nuclear, biosecurity, cyber, or counterproliferation expertise.
- Whether 2023 federal budget execution actually funded biosecurity, cyber, or CBRN-related prevention and response.
- Whether Nigeria had any 2023 1540 national implementation update, matrix revision, or assistance request that is not surfaced in the public pages inspected here.
- Whether any 2023 incident exposed failure in radiological, biological, or cyber incident response.
- Whether the nuclear-power program advanced meaningfully in 2023 beyond inherited planning.

**Corroborating Sources Opened But Not Fully Extracted**

- [State House inaugural address](https://statehouse.gov.ng/first-inaugural-address-by-president-bola-ahmed-tinubu-delivered-on-may-29-2023-at-the-eagle-square-abuja/)
- [State House New Year address](https://statehouse.gov.ng/text-of-president-bola-ahmed-tinubus-new-year-address-to-the-nation/)
- [IAEA Nigeria country profile](https://ola.iaea.org/Applications/FactSheets/Country/Detail?code=NG)
- [UN 1540 FAQ](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/faq.shtml)
- [UN 1540 matrices](https://www.un.org/en/sc/1540/national-implementation/1540-matrices.shtml)
- [NCTC books index](https://nctc.gov.ng/books/)
- [NBMA biosecurity approval page](https://nbma.gov.ng/fg-approves-a-national-biosecurity-policy-for-nigeria/)
- [NBMA unveiling page](https://nbma.gov.ng/minister-of-environment-calls-for-concerted-effort-in-the-bid-to-protect-nigerians-from-harmful-biological-agents-unveils-approved-biosecurity-policy-document/)

**Promising Leads Still Needing Inspection**

- Any Nigerian government or parliamentary document on 2023 budget execution for the National Security Adviser, NCTC, NBMA, or cyber-response agencies.
- Any 2023 or early 2024 1540 matrix update or assistance correspondence for Nigeria.
- The actual National Security Strategy 2019 PDF and National Cyber Security Policy PDF, if accessible, to inspect whether they were updated, implemented, or invoked under Tinubu.
- The National Biosecurity Policy PDF itself, to check whether implementation obligations or lead agencies were changed in 2023.
- Any IAEA or Nigerian Atomic Energy Commission update on the nuclear-power program during Tinubu’s first year.
